rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure which critical pairs respond to slope, especially the nearly coeluting late cluster. This diagnostic run will guide subsequent window trimming and temperature adjustments.
The shallower gradient did not resolve the critical clusters and incurred a time penalty. Test higher temperature at the original slope to probe selectivity changes while retaining a short run.

Probe the opposite temperature limit at the same slope to distinguish temperature-driven crossings from persistent close pairs. This completes the initial selectivity survey before refining the gradient window.

Use a narrower gradient window at the best temperature to gain separation without spending time below the main elution range. The higher starting fraction should offset the slower slope and keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope further to improve the late critical pair and the middle pair, both of which benefited from the narrower window. The predicted last peak is close to 10 minutes, so this tests the resolution–time boundary.

Lower the starting fraction to recover early-pair retention and test an intermediate temperature to shift the crowded early cluster. This slope should preserve much of the late-pair improvement while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

The first pair appears to undergo a selectivity crossing near phi0 0.10, so test a higher starting fraction rather than lowering it again. A shallower slope should improve the late cluster, with the higher start limiting the time penalty.

Test whether moving beyond the early-cluster crossing improves its separation while the shallower slope further resolves the late pair. Monitor the first three peaks closely for excessive compression at this higher starting fraction.

Shift temperature to move the early cluster away from its crossing at the best starting fraction. Raise the endpoint slightly to compensate for increased retention and keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Return to the low starting fraction, where the early cluster has a different elution pattern, and modestly reduce the slope. This should improve the late critical pair while using the time margin available in injection 3.
Refine between injections 5 and 6 to retain their resolution gains without exceeding 10 minutes. This tests a promising local compromise before exploring further selectivity changes.

Test a substantially steeper gradient to look for useful selectivity changes on the other side of the late-cluster crossings. This also establishes whether a much shorter method can compete with the current shallow-gradient optimum.

Test the low-temperature selectivity branch at phi0 0.20, where the early cluster may separate better than it did at the original starting fraction. The higher endpoint compensates for increased retention and should keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Fine-tune the best method to a slightly shallower slope while keeping the endpoint above the estimated last-peak elution fraction. This should use the remaining time margin to improve the late critical pair without a time penalty.

Test a small temperature reduction to improve the early three-peak cluster while retaining a slope close to injection 12. The predicted last peak remains near 10 minutes, allowing a direct test of this selectivity compromise.

Continue the intermediate-temperature refinement, aiming to bring the first pair above 1.5 and balance the early cluster. A slightly steeper slope compensates for the lower temperature to keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Test a distinct higher-start selectivity region with a shallower gradient, rather than making only marginal refinements. This may move the middle cluster beyond its crossing, although early-peak compression is a significant risk.

Refine the low-starting-fraction branch at a slope predicted to place the last peak almost exactly at 10 minutes. This should improve its three remaining critical pairs relative to injection 11 while preserving the well-separated early peaks.

Test whether a modest temperature reduction improves the early and middle clusters at phi0 0.25 enough to offset losses in the late pair. Injection 9 provides sufficient time margin for this selectivity test.

Lower temperature one step from injection 20 to improve the early and middle critical pairs while using its remaining time margin. This tests whether those gains outweigh the expected loss in late-pair resolution.

Test whether lower temperature restores early and middle separation at the higher starting fraction, where the 60 C run was too compressed. The steeper slope should limit the added retention and keep the last peak near 10 minutes.

Refine the competitive phi0 0.25 branch with one lower temperature step to improve the early cluster. Increase the slope slightly relative to injection 21 to offset added retention and target a last peak near 10 minutes.
Test a slightly shallower gradient near the best method, ending in a hold that may alter late-peak spacing. This checks whether additional resolution credit can outweigh any small time penalty.

Retain injection 24’s improved gradient slope but raise the endpoint so the last peak elutes during the gradient rather than the hold. This final refinement tests whether the added resolution can outweigh the small expected time penalty relative to injection 15.
